title: Al-Biruni measures the earth
hook: who measured the earth's radius and wrote a careful study of India

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Farabi, the second teacher: a city is good when its people work together toward happiness. Your line was: the virtuous city.

A man climbs a mountain with an instrument in his hands, in the land we now call Pakistan. He has already worked out how tall the mountain is. At the top, he sights along the far horizon, where the plain meets the sky, and notes how far it dips below level. That's all: a height, and one small angle. From those two things and some careful geometry, he works out the size of the whole earth. No ship sailing around it, no long journey. Just a mountain, a steady hand and patient math. His name was Abu Rayhan al-Biruni, and the mountain is only half his story.
screen: `A MOUNTAIN AND AN INSTRUMENT.` → `ONE SMALL ANGLE.` → `THE SIZE OF THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Al-Biruni wrote on astronomy, geography, minerals, calendars, and how far apart cities lay, partly so people could find the direction of Makkah for prayer. The mountain shows his habit: check the height, check the angle, check the math. The Qur'an says that God created everything by measure, and al-Biruni measured as if that were true of every stone and star. But today's deeper lesson is his other great book. He spent long stretches in India, learned Sanskrit, read the Indian sciences and scriptures in their own language, and talked with Indian scholars. Then he wrote a book about India: its beliefs, its philosophy, its astronomy, its customs and its calendar. Listen to how it begins. In his opening, al-Biruni says this is not a book of argument. He will set out what the Hindus themselves say, in their own words, as faithfully as he can, and where their thinkers resemble the Greeks, he'll show that too. He complains about earlier writers who reported on other peoples from hearsay, copying mistakes and adding insults, and he refuses to do it. Al-Biruni was a Muslim, and his book doesn't hide it. But he measured another people's thought the way he measured a mountain: carefully, without bending the numbers. That's a hard thing to do with a mountain. It's harder still with a neighbor's faith.
screen: `CHECK THE HEIGHT, THE ANGLE, THE MATH.` · `CREATED BY MEASURE.` · `IN INDIA, READING SANSKRIT.` · `NOT A BOOK OF ARGUMENT.` · then, large: `MEASURE CAREFULLY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one tradition or culture you know only from the outside, maybe from headlines or from a friend, and ask what you think you know about it. Then ask al-Biruni's question: did I learn that from them, in their own words, or from hearsay? If you pray, you can ask God for a fair mind; if not, just hold the question open.
Al-Biruni. The scholar who found the size of the earth from a mountaintop, and wrote about India from its own books, in its own words. Today's word.
Your line: measure carefully. A week of sifr, a philosopher, a hospital, two physicians, a second teacher and a measurer. That's day nine hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Muslim scholars like al-Biruni studied geography and astronomy partly to find prayer times and the direction of Makkah, and his book on India is read as a careful account of another people's thought in its own terms.

He kept his own faith out of it, so no one knew he was a Muslim.
